title: Development of Affiliative Intersubjectivity and Mindfulness in Counselor–Client Collaborative Discourses
abstract: ABSTRACT From a linguistic and humanistic frame that treats language as a window onto mind and relationship, this quasi‐experimental mixed‐methods study examines 52 counselor‐in‐training (CIT)–client dyadic sessions as the site where mindful intersubjectivity, affiliative empathy, and collaborative alliance are created in discourse. Over a metacognitively rich counseling‐techniques course, pretest–posttest analyses of metadiscourse with sentiments documented CITs’ mindful development. Reductions in directive prompting and emphatic intonation supported client autonomy and therapeutic alliance, whereas increases in affiliative disclosure, evidential justification, and attention to client feelings enhanced relational attunement and motivational‐interviewing evocation. Clients exhibited less evaluative restraint, greater positivity and evidentiality, and increased discourse quantity and quality—indicating greater openness. Clients’ mirroring of CIT mindful features reflected concerted alignment toward person‐centered communication. These patterns were associated with affinity, empathic communion, and metacognitive instruction with dyadic practice. The study offers linguistic tools for supervision and humanistic pedagogy to strengthen CIT self‐efficacy and client change.
